subject: Physics
title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
summary: In ray optics light travels in straight lines (rays). In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; in refraction Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r holds. In a denser medium (higher n) light slows down and bends towards the normal.

All mirror and lens problems use one sign convention (Cartesian: pole/optical centre at origin, direction of light positive) and two formulas: mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Magnification tells the size and whether the image is real or virtual.

Going from a denser to a rarer medium at more than the critical angle, light is completely reflected back — total internal reflection (optical fibres, sparkle of diamond, mirage). A prism deviates light and splits white light into colours (dispersion).

Lens power P = 1/f (dioptre, f in metres); powers of lenses in contact simply add. A microscope magnifies small nearby objects; a telescope increases the angle of distant objects — both use two lenses (objective + eyepiece).

formulas.name: Mirror formula and magnification
formulas.note: Sign convention: u is always negative (object in front). Concave f is negative, convex f positive.

formulas.name: Snell's law and refractive index
formulas.formula: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r;   n = c/v;   ₁n₂ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂
formulas.mistake: Frequency does NOT change between media — speed and wavelength do.

formulas.name: Apparent depth (normal view)
formulas.formula: apparent depth = real depth / n;   shift = t(1 − 1/n)
formulas.note: Viewing from the rarer medium, divide; viewing from inside the denser medium outward, multiply.

formulas.name: Critical angle and TIR
formulas.formula: sin C = 1/n  (n = denser/rarer);   TIR when light goes dense → rare with i > C
formulas.mistake: TIR happens only going from denser to rarer — never the other way.

formulas.name: Refraction at a spherical surface
formulas.note: Sign of R: positive if the centre lies on the refracted (outgoing) side.

formulas.name: Thin lens formula and magnification
formulas.mistake: The lens formula has a minus sign, unlike the mirror formula — don't mix them.

formulas.name: Lens maker's formula
formulas.when: f of a lens from its shape; effect of the surrounding medium.
formulas.note: In a medium denser than the lens, a convex lens becomes diverging.

formulas.name: Power of a lens and combination
formulas.formula: P = 1/f (f in metres, unit dioptre D);   in contact P = P₁ + P₂, 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂;   separated by d: 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/(f₁f₂)

formulas.name: Prism (angle A)
formulas.formula: r₁ + r₂ = A;   δ = i + e − A;   minimum deviation: i = e, r = A/2, n = sin[(A + δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2)
formulas.when: Deviation in a prism, finding n.
formulas.note: At minimum deviation the ray inside is parallel to the base — remember r = A/2.

formulas.name: Thin prism
formulas.mistake: Don't use this for large-angle prisms.

formulas.name: Dispersion
formulas.formula: Angular dispersion = (n_v − n_r)A;   dispersive power ω = (n_v − n_r)/(n − 1)
formulas.note: Violet bends most and red least — because n_violet > n_red.

formulas.name: Simple microscope (magnifying glass)
formulas.formula: Image at near point: m = 1 + D/f;   at infinity: m = D/f   (D = 25 cm)

formulas.name: Compound microscope
formulas.formula: m = m_o × m_e;   image at infinity (normal adjustment): m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e);   at near point: (L/f_o)(1 + D/f_e)
formulas.note: BOTH objective and eyepiece should have small f.

formulas.name: Astronomical telescope
formulas.formula: Normal adjustment: m = f_o/f_e, length = f_o + f_e;   image at near point: m = (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D)
formulas.note: Objective f is LARGE (more light, more m); eyepiece f small.

formulas.name: Mirror/lens image rules
formulas.formula: Convex mirror and concave lens: always virtual, erect, diminished image.  Real images are always inverted (m negative)
formulas.mistake: A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen — it is seen by the eye.

examples.title: Concave mirror
examples.problem: A concave mirror has f = 15 cm and the object is 20 cm away. Where is the image and what is it like?
examples.solution: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/15 + 1/20 = −1/60 ⇒ v = −60 cm (in front of the mirror, real). m = −v/u = −3 ⇒ 3 times larger, inverted.

examples.title: Convex lens
examples.problem: Convex lens f = 20 cm, object at 30 cm. Image?
examples.solution: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 ⇒ v = +60 cm (other side, real). m = v/u = −2 (twice the size, inverted).

examples.title: Lens maker: air and water
examples.problem: Biconvex lens, |R₁| = |R₂| = 20 cm, n = 1.5. f in air? f in water (n = 4/3)?

examples.title: Critical angle
examples.problem: Critical angle for glass (n = 1.5) with air?
examples.solution: sin C = 1/1.5 ⇒ C ≈ 41.8°. At larger angles light stays inside the glass.

examples.title: Depth of a tank
examples.problem: Water (n = 4/3) is 2 m deep. How deep does it look from above?
examples.solution: Apparent depth = 2/(4/3) = 1.5 m. The bottom appears raised by 0.5 m.

examples.title: n from a prism
examples.problem: An equilateral prism (A = 60°) has minimum deviation 30°. n?

examples.title: Combination of lenses
examples.problem: f₁ = +20 cm and f₂ = −40 cm in contact. Total power and focal length?

examples.title: Compound microscope
examples.problem: f_o = 1 cm, f_e = 5 cm, tube length L = 20 cm, normal adjustment (D = 25 cm). Magnifying power?

examples.title: Telescope
examples.problem: f_o = 100 cm, f_e = 5 cm, normal adjustment. Magnifying power and tube length?
examples.solution: m = f_o/f_e = 20. Length = f_o + f_e = 105 cm.

examples.title: Refraction at a curved surface
examples.problem: A point object in air is 30 cm from a convex glass surface (n = 1.5, R = 10 cm). Where is the image?
examples.solution: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R ⇒ 1.5/v + 1/30 = 0.5/10 ⇒ 1.5/v = 1/60 ⇒ v = 90 cm (inside the glass, real).

examples.title: Thin prism
examples.problem: Deviation by a thin prism with A = 4°, n = 1.5?

topics.title: Reflection by spherical mirrors
topics.explain: Concave mirror (converging) — real or virtual images; with the object inside F the image is virtual, erect and magnified (shaving mirror). Convex mirror (diverging) — always a smaller virtual image with a wide view (vehicle side mirror). Parallel rays pass through the focus F; f = R/2.

topics.title: Refraction at plane surface
topics.explain: Light bends towards the normal in a denser medium. A pencil in water looks bent, a swimming pool looks shallower, and stars twinkle (the atmosphere's changing n).

topics.title: Applications of total internal reflection
topics.explain: Optical fibres (light travels in the core by repeated TIR — internet, endoscopy), sparkle of diamond (C ≈ 24°), mirage (air layers over a hot road), totally reflecting prisms (periscopes, binoculars).

topics.title: Lenses: image formation
topics.explain: Convex lens: object beyond 2F — smaller real image; at 2F — same size; between F and 2F — larger real image; inside F — virtual, erect, magnified (magnifier). A concave lens always forms a smaller virtual image.

topics.title: Refraction through a prism
topics.explain: Deviation first decreases with i, reaches a minimum (δ_m) where i = e, then increases. Minimum deviation is used to measure n. Rainbows and prism spectra come from dispersion — VIBGYOR, violet bends most.

topics.title: Optical instruments
topics.explain: A simple microscope is a single convex lens. Compound microscope: a short-focus objective forms a real magnified image which the eyepiece magnifies further. Refracting telescope: large-focus objective. Reflecting telescope (concave mirror objective, Newtonian/Cassegrain): no chromatic aberration, a large aperture is cheaper, and images are brighter.

topics.title: The human eye (related)
topics.explain: Near point D = 25 cm, far point at infinity. Myopia (can see near): concave lens. Hypermetropia (can see far): convex lens. Presbyopia: bifocal lenses. Astigmatism: cylindrical lens.

ratta: sin C = 1/n;  glass C ≈ 42°, water ≈ 49°, diamond ≈ 24°.
n = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2);  thin prism δ = (n − 1)A.
P = 1/f (m);  in contact P = P₁ + P₂.
Microscope m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e);  telescope m = f_o/f_e, L = f_o + f_e.
Frequency doesn't change; v and λ do.
